body:
in History, Literature |   	November 6th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Even if we did­n’t make it to a screen­ing of Christo­pher Nolan’s big-screen adap­ta­tion this past sum­mer — and indeed, even if we’ve nev­er read Home­r’s orig­i­nal epic at all — we know that the Odyssey tells the sto­ry of a ten-year-long jour­ney back to Itha­ca. The nar­ra­tive’s urgency does­n’t arise from the fact that its pro­tag­o­nist, the king Odysseus, has class­es at Cor­nell to teach. In fact, he may not even be try­ing to get back to the extant Greek island cel­e­brat­ed for bear­ing that same name. So, at least, argues a recent paper by two dis­tin­guished pro­fes­sors, Cam­bridge’s James Dig­gle and the Uni­ver­si­ty of Aberdeen’s John Under­hill. You can read “Was Home­r’s Itha­ca an Island?” at the online jour­nal Antigone.
Alter­na­tive­ly, you can watch the new video from clas­si­cist-nov­el­ist Hon­or Cargill-Mar­tin above. The real Greek island of Itha­ca, or Itha­ki, with its pic­turesque ham­lets and lime­stone mono­liths, “actu­al­ly does­n’t match, pret­ty much at all, the descrip­tion that Homer gives us of Itha­ca,” she says.
Hav­ing sailed there last sum­mer, she can describe it as “an amaz­ing place, so dra­mat­ic and so evoca­tive, but in large part, that’s because the moun­tains essen­tial­ly rise straight out of the sea”  — a direct con­tra­dic­tion to Home­r’s lines about low­lands sur­round­ing a sin­gle cen­tral peak. Did he just get it wrong? Or was he tak­ing artis­tic license in order to imag­ine the kind of place from which a hero like Odysseus would come forth, despite the fact that he got his geog­ra­phy more or less right else­where?
In 2005, a man­age­ment con­sul­tant called Robert Bit­tle­stone put forth the argu­ment that Homer’s Itha­ca was actu­al­ly Pali­ki, a penin­su­la on the west­ern edge of Kefalo­nia. In order to test this the­o­ry, Bit­tle­stone brought in Dig­gle and Under­hill, his col­lab­o­ra­tors on the book Odysseus Unbound: The Search for Home­r’s Itha­ca. Now, a decade after Bit­tle­stone’s death, the oth­ers have pro­duced new geo­log­i­cal and tex­tu­al evi­dence for the Pali­ki hypoth­e­sis, not least that Homer nev­er once explic­it­ly calls Itha­ca an island, or even describes it in terms he applies to known islands. Cargill-Mar­tin finds their research “extreme­ly con­vinc­ing,” which makes you won­der: will Itha­ca take down its stat­ue of Odysseus in response? Prob­a­bly not, but at least we’ll have some­thing to talk about when we go stand before it.
via Boing Boing

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Arkivism Is an Accessible Antidote to AI with 4 Million+ Public Domain Images
description: Say you’re on the hunt for a drawing of a duck wearing a hat or a glimpse at Morocco in 1850 or a clip of people celebrating in the streets. Whate
body:
Say you’re on the hunt for a drawing of a duck wearing a hat or a glimpse at Morocco in 1850 or a clip of people celebrating in the streets. Whatever imagery it is you’re searching for, Arkivism has likely got you covered.
An accessible antidote to generative AI, Arkivism is a new public domain index that catalogs millions of artworks, illustrations, photos, video, and more from dozens of museums and archives around the world. While many digital collections exist online, the “visual library of Alexandria,” as its creator dubs it, is searchable with a phrase, a mode of research that’s become commonplace with the proliferation of chatbots. Simply describe what you’re looking for and be presented with an array of human-made results.(via Open Culture)

title: Abstract Wool Compositions Cascade from Weathered Metal in Amine El Gotaibi's Sculptures
description: “Wind knows neither North nor South. Neither East nor West. It moves freely across territories, indifferent to the categories that divide them,” A
body:
“Wind knows neither North nor South. Neither East nor West. It moves freely across territories, indifferent to the categories that divide them,” Amine El Gotaibi says. The Moroccan artist positions nature’s apathy toward national boundaries as an entry point for unraveling the forces that shape our perceptions and memories of a place.
El Gotaibi’s most recent body of work is on view this month at Southern Guild. Presented in an exhibition titled Wind From the North, a suite of sculptures made of metal and wool speak to the tensions between the land and the state and the ways we mark change. Many of the works emerge from panels of copper or steel weathered to reveal the oxidized patinas only possible with time. Affixed to these aged backdrops are tufts of beige and rust-colored fibers, which are either wound into tightly knotted tufts or left free-flowing. 
“Desert Wind” (2026), Corten steel and wool, 200 x 130 x 50 centimeters
Echoing the undulating terrain of mountains and the countryside, the cascading fibers tether to the artist’s interest in examining the landscapes of his home country and Northern Africa, more broadly. Wool is significant in the highlands, as textile production is one of the oldest craft traditions in this part of the continent. For El Gotaibi, this material significance directly links to his desire to challenge the idea that Africa’s cultural contributions are most likely to emerge from the central and south. 
Instead, Wind from the North, an exhibition statement says, “extends this proposition beyond fixed coordinates, imagining geography as porous and interconnected, shaped as much by what passes through it as by the lines drawn around it.”
Wind From the North is on view through January 9 in New York. Find more from El Gotaibi on Instagram.

title: What Else Could It Mean? A Book Surveys the Playful, Iconoclastic Works of James Wines
description: It’s not uncommon for artists and architects to espouse a desire for breaking conventions and pushing boundaries, but so few have embodied such a
body:
It’s not uncommon for artists and architects to espouse a desire for breaking conventions and pushing boundaries, but so few have embodied such a mandate as James Wines. An unparalleled devotee of wit and play, Wines is behind SITE (Sculpture in the Environment), a New York-based studio founded in 1970 with a portfolio that spans commercial construction, urban infrastructure, public art, and more. No matter the project, SITE’s approach is rooted in questioning the division between art and architecture and defying expectations.
In the preface to the new book, What Else Could It Mean?, Wines describes how he spent months in Rome after college soaking in the religious designs and civically unified architecture, which inspired what became his signature mode of working. When he returned to the U.S. to continue teaching at New York University, he asked his students to create with the opposite approach, one that tapped into a fractured and diverse contemporary landscape. “What else could it mean?” became a driving ethos that centered around “architecture as a critique of itself, as an inversion of design expectations, as humorous insights and the absorption of context as a motivating source of ideas,” he writes.
Grand opening of the Best Notch Showroom
Published by Skira, What Else Could It Mean? showcases dozens of projects from the SITE oeuvre. The most iconic of the studio’s works are designs for BEST Products Company, a big box store that operated for four decades. Owners Sydney and Frances Lewis tapped Wines to create unconventional structures for their showrooms, which included a building that appeared to sink into the ground at an angle and another that split open as the base fractured from the rest of the facade.
The BEST designs are just a piece of SITE’s broader commentary on commercialization. There’s also “Ghost Parking Lot,” an enormous, immovable public art project in Hamden, Connecticut, that buried twenty cars beneath asphalt. Forever halted outside the shopping mall, the immobile vehicles became ghostly signals of endless consumption and urban sprawl.
What Else Could It Mean? collects Wines’ drawings, renderings, and writings across five decades, presenting these rarely seen documents alongside archival photos of realized projects. SITE’s ethos has particular relevancy today, especially as it challenges the inherent accessibility of art and architecture and advocates for a more democratic approach to collective life. Designer and curator Phillip Denny writes in the introduction: 

These are works that engage their context, invite participation, and reward curiosity regardless of one’s background. It is art and architecture for the popular public that anyone can stop in front of, be surprised by, laugh at, and think about without a guidebook. Often ironic but never cynical, always generous and ecumenical, SITE created art where people least expected to find it, in the “junk-culture world of the commercial strip and suburban sprawl.”

Get your copy of What Else Could It Mean? on Bookshop, and explore more of SITE’s works on its website.

title: Met Gala’s New Theme Is So Basic
description:

body:
Daily Newsletter
                Brancusi at MoMA, trouble at Pace, a rediscovered Georgia O'Keeffe painting, and The Met presents the biggest rescission indicator yet.  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Jackson Pollock at The Met, Roy Lichtenstein at the Whitney, and Constantin Brancusi at the Museum of Modern Art — our critic Aruna D'Souza is tired of this dead-White-men fest. That said, she still has a soft spot for Brancusi. She went to see the Romanian artist’s solo show at MoMA, and she has some thoughts.  Speaking of dead White blokes, visitors to the MFA Boston will soon be able to watch a live conservation of Dutch painter Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy’s “The Six Founders of the Amsterdam Wine Guild” (1625). Watching paint dry never sounded so appealing.In living-White-men news, Pace Gallery, owned by father-and-son duo Arne and Marc Glimcher, has reported steep losses. Meanwhile, a recently rediscovered Georgia O'Keeffe painting is heading to auction and might sell for millions.  But if that’s all too exciting, get a load of the Met Gala's new “everyday” theme.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 

	
		
			At MoMA, Brancusi Is Lost in Space
		
	
	
		Let’s get one thing out of the way first: For all my weariness about how canonical dead White men are STILL. CONSISTENTLY. CENTERED in museum exhibitions — even after said museums have publicly taken pains to expand collections, hire curators with broad expertise and interests, and invite new audiences into their spaces — I have ZERO complaints about putting on a Constantin Brancusi exhibition. Even in fall 2026, when the city’s three major museums have turned themselves over to Brancusi, Lichtenstein, and Pollock simultaneously. (I will go to my grave insisting that it should have been a Krasner show.) 
      	
      That said, the work of this particular canonical dead White man is glorious, and continues to resonate with contemporary artists: His name has come up consistently in interviews with sculptors this past year, whether Rodney McMillian or Martin Puryear or a number of others I’ve talked to. Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio at the Museum of Modern Art is a great reminder of why.| Aruna D’Souza

title: Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center
description:
News
                Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding even
body:
News
                Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Pablo Helguera (photo You Hah Kim, courtesy Vera List Center for Art and Politics)
    
        
            Artist, educator, and writer Pablo Helguera has been appointed as the new director of the New School's Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC), succeeding Senior Director and Chief Curator Carin Kuoni, who steered the arts-driven research center for 22 years. Helguera was also tapped as the director of the university's art collection, which consists of over 2,000 postwar and contemporary works.Having entered the new role this Monday, November 2, Helguera takes the reins after six years of serving as an assistant professor and director of the Arts Management and Entrepreneurship graduate program at the New School's College of Performing Arts. Helguera was previously the director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade.As an artist, Helguera centers social engagement through public performance and installation, archival findings, pedagogical practices, and traditional media. Among his most famous projects is “The School of Panamerican Unrest” (2006), a cross-continental road trip from Anchorage, Alaska, to Ushuaia, capital of Argentina's southernmost Tierra del Fuego province, that culminated in over 100 public engagement events across 25 cities in 20 countries. Helguera is also known for developing Librería Donceles, a traveling used bookstore with thousands of Spanish-language texts that visited 13 countries. The social, ideological, and cultural frameworks of language are prominent themes that Helguera explores in his practice, which coalesces with his roles in education and public programming. He became a Guggenheim Fellow in 2008, and additional recognitions include support from the Franklin Furnace Archive, Art Matters, and Blade of Grass; a Creative Capital grant; and an honorary doctorate from the Kansas City Art Institute.

title: DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch
description:

body:
Trump Administration
                A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A protestor holds a sign that calls to stop the construction "arch of stupid." (all photos Emma Cieslik/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project. Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction. At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch. Ann Wright and Ellen Barfield hold their signs before the protest.
